articles.title: Conspiracy theory communication framing and support for antidemocratic behavior
articles.abstract: Many politicians use conspiracy theories (CTs) to win electoral support and justify antidemocratic policies. How do individuals evaluate this strategy? We theorize and show that variation in CT communication frames affects individuals’ willingness to endorse antidemocratic policies and politicians. Politicians who explicitly appeal to a CT earn greater support for antidemocratic behavior than those using implicit appeals. However, this effect primarily occurs for novel CTs lacking partisan cues. Over time, as CTs become more politicized, they lose their mobilizational capacity and can reduce support for CT‐wielding politicians—even among co‐partisans. Three preregistered survey experiments surrounding the 2023 parliamentary and 2025 presidential elections in Poland, and survey data from 21 countries, provide empirical support for our theory. Ultimately, we show that CTs alone are not always enough to justify attacks on democratic norms and institutions to the public.

articles.title: Do Politicians’ Errors in Understanding Public Opinion Persist When They Encounter Individual Constituents?
articles.authors: JACK LUCAS, LIOR SHEFFER, NOAM TITELMAN
articles.abstract: When thinking about public opinion, politicians commonly exhibit three general perceptual errors: a tendency to overestimate their constituents’ conservatism ( conservative bias ), a tendency to hold more accurate knowledge of privileged constituents than constituents in general ( privilege bias ), and a tendency to overestimate how much their constituents share their views ( projection bias ). Studies documenting these patterns invariably rely on assessing politicians’ perceptions of aggregated public opinion. In practice, however, politicians heavily prioritize and rely on the opinions of individual constituents, raising concerns about the external validity of these findings. Thus, in this article, we explore whether politicians’ common perceptual errors persist when they think about specific individual constituents, rather than aggregate public opinion. We assign more than 1,400 Canadian politicians to predict the ideology and issue positions of more than 4,000 randomly generated citizen profiles that vary by a host of salient sociodemographic and political factors. We then compare their evaluations to estimates of these citizens’ real-life positions drawn from a general population survey. We find that politicians do not exhibit conservative bias or privilege bias when making inferences about individual constituents. However, even when thinking about individual constituents, projection bias persists, and the perception errors it creates are amplified when politicians are more similar to their constituents. We discuss the implications of these findings for theories of political representation.

articles.title: Blood is Still Thicker Than Water: A Response to Lin’s Reappraisal and Reflections on Historical Political Economy
articles.abstract: A recent reappraisal by Lin expands Wang’s (2022, American Political Science Review 116, 896–910) dataset and questions the robustness of its main finding. In this response, I clarify broader challenges of measurement, case selection, and inference in historical political economy. I show that my original finding—that kinship-network concentration is negatively associated with support for state-building reforms—remains robust across multiple coding strategies. I also acknowledge that two high-leverage cases, the Lü brothers, matter for inference; rather than treating them as removable anomalies, I argue that their extreme values are theoretically meaningful features of kinship-network structure. Finally, I engage Lin’s regional interpretation and show that regional status competition does not account for the observed relationship once measurement and estimation issues are addressed. More broadly, this exchange illustrates how transparent measurement and sustained dialogue between quantitative and qualitative evidence can generate cumulative knowledge from fragmentary historical archives.

articles.title: Merit or Whiteness? Tracing Racial Bias in the Selection of Individual UN Human Rights Experts
articles.abstract: Do race or merit make an international expert? While existing research has uncovered epistemic biases related to gender and professions, racial bias in international organisations’ expert selection has not been captured. We argue that signalling whiteness is central to the certification of expertise because expert status is built on racialised structures of epistemic power. Examining individual-level data from 2,053 applications and selection outcomes across several stages in 124 decision rounds between 2011 and 2024 for the United Nations’ Special Procedures, we show that expert selection is subject to racial bias when candidates are chosen for in-person interviews and how markers of whiteness and merit overlap. We also find that non-white experts can increase their chances of being selected when they possess higher merit-related credentials than their white counterparts. Our research informs scholarship on racism in international relations, the production of expertise in international organisations, and human rights politics.

articles.title: Regional Deprivation, Individual Prospects, and Political Resentment
articles.authors: Giovanni Facchini, Anja Neundorf, Sergi Pardos-Prado, Cecilia Testa
articles.abstract: Regional economic conditions are well-established determinants of the geography of political resentment. However, regions are not homogeneous, and the mechanisms through which local economies affect individual political attitudes are unclear. We argue that feelings of relative deprivation are shaped by how personal prospects are tied to regional conditions, and that the interaction between subjective individual and regional deprivation affects perceptions of shared struggle and systemic unfairness. Through a large-scale survey experiment in Britain addressing geographical self-selection, we provide causal evidence that poor individuals in poor regions express political resentment, whereas in affluent regions the political attitudes of poor and wealthy individuals are indistinguishable. Our findings stress (1) the importance of egocentric mechanisms whereby local economies shape individual prospects; (2) the significance of subjective beliefs over objective information on deprivation; (3) the mobilization potential of highlighting regional deprivation by political entrepreneurs; and (4) the relevance of place-based policies to mitigate political discontent.

articles.title: Breaking into the Public Sphere: How Protest Tactics Shape Media Visibility
articles.abstract: Getting heard is a crucial first step for protesters to influence policy and public opinion. How can protest organisers boost their coverage in the media? This study provides new evidence on this question, based on a decade of UK environmental and economic protests from 2010 to 2020 ( N = 1,708). Relying on protest groups’ social media streams as trace data, I introduce a computer-assisted method for constructing a media-independent protest event dataset. Using a ‘within-group’ design, I provide a sharper test of the causal effects of tactical choices compared to previous studies. I find that confrontational elements, such as disruption and arrests, are the strongest predictors, more than doubling the expected magnitude of coverage. I also find that right-leaning (ideologically unsympathetic) outlets are more responsive to confrontational elements than left-leaning (ideologically sympathetic) outlets, which suggests that disruptive tactics affect the composition as well as the size of a protest’s audience.

articles.title: Many ways to hate: varieties of negative partisanship and their correlates
Public support for undermining executive accountability in times of crisis
articles.authors: Erica De Bruin, Calvert W. Jones
articles.abstract: Major crises have historically resulted in the expansion of executive power and undermining of democratic accountability. Yet, we know surprisingly little about which types of crises generate the greatest risk and which types of accountability-undermining actions – often justified by executives in the context of crisis – are most likely to gain public acceptance. To explore these questions, we field an original conjoint experiment over a large and nationally representative sample of Americans. Although respondents are generally averse to actions undermining accountability, they also reveal substantial variation in their degree of aversion – across both crisis and action types. We demonstrate that they are most likely to tolerate such actions after physical security crises, compared to socio-economic and political crises, and also most likely to tolerate actions undermining horizontal accountability, compared to vertical or diagonal. To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first to empirically demonstrate these hierarchies of risk, shedding light on how antecedent conditions as well as agentic choices can differentially shape public support for undermining executive accountability.

articles.title: Expert surveys and the ideational approach to populism: The impact of conceptualization and aggregation
articles.authors: Nina Wiesehomeier, Saskia P. Ruth-Lovell, Matthew Singer
articles.abstract: We contrast the conceptualization, operationalization, and measurement of party-level populism in three major expert survey projects: the Populism and Political Parties Expert Survey, the Political Representation, Executives, and Political Parties Survey, and the Varieties of Party Identity and Organization Survey (V-Party). Although all three adopt the ideational approach to populism, they differ in how the concept is translated into rating scales, the number and content of items, the specification of scale endpoints, and the aggregation procedures used to construct a single populism index. Drawing on 125 political parties from 23 European countries, we examine whether these methodological choices affect how parties are scored and how robust resulting rankings and classifications are to alternative aggregation rules. We compare each project’s original index with four weakest-link aggregation rules − minimum, multiplication, harmonic mean, and geometric mean − to assess the sensitivity of the resulting populism indices to compensatory versus non-compensatory aggregation assumptions. We find that aggregation choices can produce substantial differences, with the classical minimum function diverging most strongly from the original indices and from partially compensatory rules. While the most and least populist parties are identified consistently across aggregation methods, parties located in the middle of the scale are frequently reclassified, suggesting that methodological choices can matter most for empirically ‘intermediate’ cases. We further examine the inferential consequences by replicating a recent study, showing that aggregation rules can alter estimated relationships involving populist appeals, particularly when conclusions hinge on moderate, mainstream parties. We conclude with recommendations for the development and use of expert surveys.

articles.title: Environmental clash? The environmental dimension and electoral preferences in six European democracies
articles.authors: Silvia Bolgherini, Luca Carrieri, Matteo Giardiello
articles.abstract: The political debate over environmental issues in Europe has grown increasingly contested and likely influences voting behaviour. Yet most research treats environmental voting as a single environmental protection versus economic growth dichotomy. This article reconceptualises the “environmental issue” as a composite “environmental dimension” integrating socio-economic trade-offs concerning household consumption, public services, economic growth, and employment. We rely on original survey data from six EU member states (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain and Sweden), testing the association between this composite dimension and the vote intentions for European party families. By performing logistic regression models separately for each party family, our findings yield two main results. First, anti-environmental attitudes are systematically correlated with the electoral preferences of Radical Right parties. Second, pro-environmental orientations are associated with voting intentions for Greens, Social-Democrats, Radical Left, and also Christian Democratic/Conservative parties. In brief, the environmental dimension generates widespread and two-sided electoral responses among supporters of different party families, constituting a significant correlate of their voting preferences.

articles.title: How local rivalry shapes party systems. Perspectives on territorial cleavages
articles.abstract: What do theories on social cleavages, political institutions and multi-level party systems teach us about local elections? This manuscript extends this literature by considering elections across multiple levels. It argues that, in countries with territorial cleavages, competition in local elections can structure the party system: in places where the minority is the majority, multiple rival parties from the same minority groups will emerge, and these parties may also become active in the national arena. The empirical analysis first provides a comparative analysis of the representation of ethnic minorities in the national arena in 62 multiethnic democracies. This is complemented by an analysis of local elections in six democracies with significant minority-majority strongholds. Results highlight the importance of local politics as a driver of electoral competition, as well as the role of non-partisans and local groups in the local arena.

articles.title: Policing the coalition bargain: The ministerial committee on legislation and private members’ bills in Israel, 1999–2018
articles.abstract: How do coalition governments manage parliamentary initiatives that may challenge their policy commitments? This article examines Israel’s Ministerial Committee on Legislation (MCL) as an executive arena for reviewing private members’ bills (PMBs). Reinterpreting 11,446 decisions across six Knesset terms (1999–2018), it identifies a sustained shift from rejection to postponement: decisions expressing support or opposition fell from 97.2 to 35.7%. Deferrals rose from 2.8 to 64.3%, becoming the largest decision category in the 20 th Knesset. They emerge as a potential latent veto that can preserve coalition flexibility while obscuring responsibility for blocked initiatives. Decisions on opposition PMBs further show that agenda control includes accommodation as well as exclusion. These patterns illuminate how cabinet committees can manage parliamentary initiatives through postponement, conditionality, and selective support. The article extends coalition-policing theory to executive screening of private member bills and highlights the tension between coalition coordination, transparency, and parliamentary autonomy.

articles.title: The devil is in the divisor: Deviations from proportionality in Dutch municipal coalition negotiations, 1998 – 2022
articles.abstract: Under what circumstances do parties get a share of executive posts that is not directly proportional to their legislative seats? While there is strong empirical support for Gamson’s law, i.e., the distribution of executive posts in a coalition is directly proportional to the negotiating parties’ number of legislative seats, we know little about when deviations from this pattern occur. To get a grip on these deviations, we study coalition negotiations at the Dutch local level between 1998 and 2022. Major deviations from Gamson’s law are rare, and most deviations occur because no strictly proportional solution was available. Small parties are usually overrepresented and large parties are usually underrepresented. The norm of proportionality is very strong: divisor methods that distribute executive posts over parties according to their legislative seats help predict how these posts are distributed. There is no consistent evidence that parties’ bargaining power affects the direction or size of divergences.

articles.title: Uncertain Performance: How to Quantify Uncertainty and Draw Test Sets When Evaluating Classifiers
articles.abstract: Supervised machine learning has become increasingly popular in social science research, often employing classifiers to measure political constructs. Although evaluating classifiers on a test set is critical for establishing their validity, guidance on how to conduct such evaluation is limited. In particular, researchers have paid insufficient attention to the variance of performance metrics estimated on test sets. This article demonstrates that typically sized test sets yield highly noisy and often uninformative estimates of classifier performance, particularly for imbalanced tasks—common in social science applications like identifying hateful or emotional speech—where one outcome class is rare. To address this issue, this article introduces methods to quantify uncertainty in performance estimates based on their sampling distribution and validated with simulations. It also introduces a design-based approach in political science to enhance statistical precision when evaluating classifiers: efficient stratified sampling based on the outcome’s predicted probability. Simulations using synthetic and real data show that this strategy meaningfully reduces the variance of performance estimates, especially in imbalanced tasks, while ensuring that they remain consistent. Finally, the article illustrates how to calculate the test set size required to achieve a desired level of statistical precision. Accompanying statistical software enables researchers to easily implement these methods.

articles.title: The Earth Moves, but So Does the Bias: Systematic Upward Bias of the Wasserstein (Earth-Mover) Distance and Permutation-Based Null Calibration
articles.abstract: The earth mover’s distance (EMD) is gaining increasing interest among political scientists for assessing similarity in preference distributions. Existing applications predominantly involve relatively large samples and low-dimensional response spaces, which can mitigate finite-sample distortions. However, empirical EMD remains biased upward due to sampling variation in empirical probability measures. This problem is often overlooked and becomes especially severe in high-dimensional or sparse settings, including conjoint distributions that serve as an illustrative example in this article. As political scientists are broadening their use cases of EMD, this article cautions against interpreting standard bootstrap uncertainty bounds as a correction for the upward bias of empirical EMD. It proposes a permutation-based null calibration framework for more robust hypothesis testing. As a non-parametric approach, it frees researchers from making directional or distributional shape assumptions. While alternative estimators require these rigid assumptions to correct for upward bias, political science data often fail to meet them in practice. Through four sets of Monte Carlo simulations, this article demonstrates the utility of this framework. The proposed approach also applies more generally to empirical comparisons of two probability distributions defined on a common metric space, provided that the ground distance between support points is substantively meaningful.

articles.title: Correcting Bias When Using Latent Regressors
articles.abstract: Many core concepts in political science are latent and therefore can only be measured with error. Measurement error in a predictor attenuates slope coefficient estimates in regression, often biasing them toward zero. We show that widely used strategies for correcting attenuation bias—including instrumental variables and the method of composition—are themselves biased when applied to latent regressors, often performing worse than simple regression ignoring the measurement error altogether. We derive a correlation-based correction using split-sample measurement strategies. Rather than assuming a particular estimation strategy for the latent trait, our approach is modular and can be easily deployed with a wide variety of latent-variable measurement strategies, including additive score, factor or machine-learning models; it requires no joint estimation while yielding consistent slopes under standard assumptions. Simulations and applications show stronger relationships after our correction, sometimes by as much as 50%. Open-source software implements the procedure. Results underscore that latent predictors demand tailored error correction; otherwise, conventional practice can exacerbate bias.

articles.title: Toward a global political psychology: James H. Liu's legacy in global consciousness and global social identification
articles.abstract: Political challenges such as climate change and pandemics require cooperation across national and cultural boundaries. Former Political Psychology editor‐in‐chief, Professor James H. Liu's work on global consciousness examined how people might recognize this interdependence while remaining attentive to cultural difference and unequal relations of power. In this introduction, we situate global consciousness within debates about globalization and cosmopolitanism, distinguish it from related forms of global social identification and review the cross‐cultural and behavioral research that developed from Prof. Liu's theoretical work. We then introduce four contributions that examine the distribution of global identifications across societies, their relationship with concern for global issues, the role of socioeconomic context in environmental engagement, and the conceptualization and measurement of global consciousness. Together, the contributions challenge assumptions that global orientations are chiefly products of affluent Western societies. They also show why understanding their consequences requires attention to the contexts in which people express them. We conclude by considering how Prof. Liu's legacy can guide a political psychology that is global in both its subject matter and its approach to theory building.

articles.title: Vox employee: green workers and corporate climate action
articles.authors: Jared Cory, Michael Lerner, Iain Osgood
articles.abstract: Public opinion— vox populi —influences political outcomes through voting, protest, and civil society, but can it also do so through corporations’ political behavior? Climate policy offers a crucial test for this question because support for climate action varies widely across the employed public, and corporate employers are heavily involved in both private and public climate governance. To explore how workers’ climate attitudes— vox employee —shape the climate policies of corporations, we build the first index of workforce sentiment toward climate policy. We show that firms with pro-climate workforces are more likely to make net-zero commitments, hire sustainability officers, publicly report their emissions, and join pro-climate corporate coalitions. Our findings describe an underappreciated channel through which public opinion influences politics: the political behavior of the public’s employers.

articles.title: Introduction: Swimming Against the Stream: James C. Scott and American Political Science
articles.abstract: American political science lost one of its most influential scholars on July 19, 2024. James C. Scott, Yale’s Sterling Professor Emeritus of Political Science, was not only a major figure within his home discipline. His work also shaped conversations across the social sciences and beyond, including anthropology, sociology, history, agrarian studies, geography, and Southeast Asian studies.

articles.title: Polarization and Disorder in America’s Trade and Climate Politics
articles.authors: Anil Menon, Iain Osgood, Nicole Wu
articles.abstract: The world faces failing cooperation and decaying order in both international trade and climate-change mitigation, each intensified by diminishing US cooperation. Building on previous literature, we trace a common cause of American abnegation of leadership in these areas: partisan polarization. Polarization makes solving the redistributive, cooperative, and intergenerational components of these problems harder by devaluing solidarity, trust, and the future. Using original survey data, we examine polarization in US public opinion on trade and climate across three domains: on domestic regulation, where non-cooperation in these issues begins; on global cooperation, where these issues are collectively addressed; and on green industrial policy, where these issues converge. Our data show that polarization in these areas is stably significant but also responsive to recent political and policy changes. Given America’s historic role in building the current international order, further polarization will likely degrade order with potentially harmful effects.

articles.title: A House Divided: Agricultural Producers’ Attitudes Toward International Trade
articles.authors: Evren Çelik Wiltse, Filip Viskupič, David L. Wiltse
articles.abstract: Trade policy in the United States began to change rapidly during the two Trump administrations as higher tariffs dominated policy agendas and voters increasingly favored protectionism over globalization. These protectionist tendencies may be easier to explain in sectors that experienced deindustrialization and offshoring. However, protectionism is more difficult to explain for sectors that greatly benefited from global trade. Agriculture in the United States stands out among the “winners” of globalization. Although farm incomes consistently increased due to the global markets, agricultural producers leaned heavily toward anti-trade candidates. To examine the nuances of preferences about international trade within the sector, we conducted a survey of agricultural producers in April 2022 in South Dakota. Results of a series of ordered logistic regression models with robust standard errors reveal that there was statistically significant variation among the farmers based on what they produced. We conclude that the “new” new trade theory is a good framework that captures this within-sector variation in trade preferences.

articles.title: The Political Art of James C. Scott: Making Waves
articles.abstract: James C. Scott was a contrarian who questioned the benefits of strong states and who praised the political astuteness and agility of marginalized and impoverished people. He used metaphors, allegories, and legends to advance controversial ideas about the unpredictability of nature and society, the omnipresence of deception within governing institutions, and the secret political activities of downtrodden people. By drawing attention to wall graffiti, limericks, sidewalk gossip, and other phenomena seldom examined by political scientists, Scott’s art expanded and enriched the study of grassroots politics. However, he also neglected certain topics—including the forms of argumentation and the ways of listening—by which oppressed individuals transformed their heterogeneous opinions about circumstances, threats, and possibilities into common views, sentiments of solidarity, and springboards for collective action.

articles.title: Teaching Experimental Inference Through a Null Result: Diagnosing “Failure” in a Conjoint Study of Police Accountability
articles.authors: Courtenay R. Monroe, Sophia Hatz, Kristine Eck
articles.abstract: Null results are common in research but rarely central in classroom instruction. Diagnosing and interpreting null effects is fundamental to causal inference and research transparency. This article presents a classroom-ready case study based on a conjoint survey experiment examining public expectations about police accountability mechanisms. Although our study was theoretically motivated and well powered, it produced null findings. We use this case to model a diagnostic framework based on Kane (2025), guiding students through assessments of common pitfalls in survey research: inattentiveness, non-compliance, heterogeneous effects, and statistical power. By reframing null findings as analytic opportunities, instructors can strengthen students’ understanding of experimental inference.

articles.title: Critical Hermeneutics, Shared Standards, and Scott’s Contrarianism
articles.abstract: If James C. Scott practiced an art of not being governed by the disciplinary standards of political science, then what type of art was this? What made it disruptive? And what are its implications for the science of political inquiry? This contribution to the symposium on his work addresses these questions via a reading of Weapons of the Weak: Everyday Forms of Peasant Resistance (Scott 1985). Although commentary on Weapons has noted that it is unusual for being an ethnography by a political scientist at a time when the discipline was headed in other directions, the book’s significance lies in its underlying concern to foreground meaning—which is to say, in its hermeneutic qualities.

articles.title: Against the Grain: James C. Scott and the Narrowing of American Political Science
articles.abstract: This article traces James C. Scott’s intellectual journey against the grain of American political science. Drawing on his writing and my own work on the history of the discipline, I show how Scott’s interpretive approach diverged from the priorities of the National Science Foundation (NSF), the discipline’s dominant patron throughout his six-decade career. Whereas NSF-funded studies such as the World Values Survey sought universal metrics and cross-national comparability, Scott emphasized local knowledge and intersubjective meaning. In Seeing Like a State , Scott invited readers to turn his argument about the state’s compulsion for legibility against “a certain kind of reductive social science.” I take up his invitation, showing not only that the NSF privileged the types of legibility projects Scott critiqued but also that its efforts to remake the discipline bear a family resemblance to the pathologies of “high modernism.” A state agency elevated a narrow range of approaches as the authoritative form of political inquiry, entrenched an epistemological monoculture that devalued local knowledge, and “disciplined” a field uniquely positioned to produce knowledge critical of the state. This history illuminates enduring tensions between different modes of knowledge production and the cost of institutionalizing one at the expense of others. Scott’s early work, funded by the NSF in a rare exception to its orthodoxy, underscores the road not taken: a pluralist approach that could have nurtured other ways of seeing politics.

articles.title: Two Cheers for Political Science: A Scottian Approach to the Discipline
articles.abstract: James C. Scott was famously and publicly skeptical not only of disciplinary boundaries but also of the very idea that he might be a political scientist. Even so, he not only served out his career in political science departments but also published (more than once!) in the flagship American Political Science Review. It is incontrovertible that late-in-life, anarchism-cheering Scott was a very different scholar from his more youthful, behavioralist self. As he shifted his analytical gaze from early postcolonial Malaysian bureaucrats to early-capitalist Malaysian peasants, and thence farther afield, his approach to power broadly changed. Yet, it would be a mistake—however much Scott himself might encourage it—to recast him as something other than a political scientist. Rather, his presence in the discipline confirms the breadth of what “counts” as political science, in ways both inherently intellectually fruitful and validating for area specialists and others who are keen to spread their scholarly wings.

articles.title: Mandatory Civic Education in Public Universities: The Case of the South Carolina REACH Act
articles.abstract: During the past decade, state legislators have become increasingly involved in decisions about the types of classes that are taught at public universities. One area of growing interest for legislators, particularly Republicans, is courses on the founding principles of the US government. Although founding-documents laws have passed in several states, little is known about the level of public support for this type of legislation despite the implementation costs, extra requirements for students, and challenges to academic freedom that they may present. This study analyzes data from a 2024 general-population survey of South Carolina to examine support for the state’s 2021 Reinforcing College Education on America’s Constitutional Heritage (REACH) Act. Our results indicate strong public support for this legislation and demonstrate that partisan identification and conservative attitudes about race are key factors in explaining support.

articles.title: Thinking about Names, Numbers, and Categories with James C. Scott
articles.abstract: Across his work, James C. Scott theorized naming and counting. This article explores potential links of those acts with category-making.

articles.title: Teaching James C. Scott’s Hidden Transcripts to Advanced Undergraduates
articles.abstract: In this essay, I recount how I used Hidden Transcripts to teach advanced undergraduates about different ways of understanding theory and evidence. Quotations from students’ research papers illustrate their use of Scott as well as his impact on their thinking and analysis. I hope in this way to honor Scott’s work and legacy—as a man whose voracious appetite for ideas stands as a model of the academic intellectual.

articles.title: Covid-19, lockdown stringency, and terrorist attacks
Beyond Harberger: three postulates for economic policy assessments and recommendations
Sustaining democracy under the shadow of force
articles.authors: Zhaotian Luo, Adam Przeworski, Hongding Zhu
articles.abstract: Democracy faces two threats: incumbents may peacefully monopolize office, or political factions may seek power through violent conflict. Using a dynamic model, the authors examine some conditions under which democracy is sustainable against both threats. Two parties vie for office under the shadow of force. To resolve conflict, the incumbent can share revenue as well as hold competitive elections: each time, it chooses the probability of losing the next election and redistributes revenue. Elections enable the incumbent to concede control over revenue over time but come with regular risks of defeat. Democracy is sustainable if the economic stakes in elections are neither too low nor too high, while the military strength is sufficiently balanced between the two parties. When the stakes are high, democracy may be sustained only with civilian control of the military or programmatic transfers.
